description: Curated vocabulary for war and violence reporting and essential time expressions, prepositions, durations and word families.

units.title: Unit 59 — War and violence
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 124–125 (PDF pages 125–126).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe soldiers, armies, defending and protecting people, wars, battles and enemies using neutral vocabulary.
Distinguish noun and verb uses of attack, search and escape and form related word families.
Understand neutral reporting language for explosions, injuries, casualties, missing people and searches.
Use die, dead, death, kill, shot and shoot correctly and distinguish war from battle.
Contrast damaged with destroyed and use natural phrases such as take place and get away.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The army helped to protect people during the emergency.
items.note: An organised military force; army is a collective noun.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: Several soldiers were sent to help after the storm.
items.note: A member of an army.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The police found a gun near the building.
items.note: A weapon that shoots bullets.

items.pt: portar uma arma de fogo; carregar uma arma
items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The guards were carrying guns at the entrance.
items.note: Carry means have something with you; it does not mean fire it.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: Two people carried the injured man to safety.
items.note: Take or hold something while moving.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: Protecting the community is an important responsibility.
items.note: Something that it is your duty to do or deal with.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The soldiers defended the village from attack.
items.note: Verb often followed by an object and from or against.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The team was responsible for the defence of the town.
items.note: British spelling of the noun related to defend; American spelling: defense.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: Emergency workers helped protect the residents.
items.note: Keep someone or something safe from harm or danger.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The families needed protection from further attacks.
items.note: Noun related to protect; often protection from something.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The attack took place near the border.
items.note: Noun or verb; an attempt to hurt or damage someone or something.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: Officials reported a violent attack outside the town.
items.note: Collocation with the adjective violent.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The soldiers tried to avoid the enemy's position.
items.note: A person or force that is fighting against another.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The two groups fought for several hours.
items.note: The past tense is fought; the word can be a verb or noun.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The soldiers were ordered to fight the enemy.
items.note: Direct-object pattern: fight someone; fight against someone is also possible.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The war lasted for several years.
items.note: A large-scale armed conflict, often involving countries or organised groups.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: The battle ended after three hours.
items.note: A particular period of fighting; a battle may be part of a longer war.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: Community leaders asked for an end to the violence.
items.note: Behaviour intended to hurt or kill someone; an uncountable noun.

items.section: A · The job of the army
items.example: A violent incident was reported overnight.
items.note: Adjective related to violence; pronounced with three syllables in careful speech.

items.example: The police discovered an unexploded bomb.
items.note: An explosive device; the final b is silent.

items.example: The report described the bombing of a building.
items.note: A noun for an attack involving bombs.

items.example: A bomb exploded in an empty field.
items.note: An intransitive verb; past tense exploded.

items.example: Residents heard an explosion near the station.
items.note: Noun related to explode; not the same as the verb.

items.pt: ser morto; perder a vida devido a um ataque
items.example: Several people were killed in the incident.
items.note: Passive expression used when an event or someone causes death.

items.example: The explosion killed several animals near the road.
items.note: Transitive: someone or something kills another person or animal.

items.example: Two people were injured when the wall fell.
items.note: Passive form; injured does not necessarily mean killed.

items.example: The injured passengers were taken to hospital.
items.note: Adjective describing someone who has been hurt.

items.word: in the heart of the city
items.pt: no coração da cidade; no centro da cidade
items.example: The museum is in the heart of the city.
items.note: In the heart of describes a central location; it is not a reference to the organ.

items.example: The storm destroyed several old buildings.
items.note: Damage so badly that something no longer exists or cannot be used; stronger than damage.

items.example: The fire caused enormous destruction.
items.note: Noun related to destroy; can refer to physical or environmental damage.

items.example: The accident damaged the front of the car.
items.note: Something can be damaged without being completely destroyed.

items.example: Rescue teams searched the area for survivors.
items.note: Verb and noun; search an area, or search for a person or thing.

items.example: Officers continued to search for the missing child.
items.note: Use search for the person or thing that you hope to find.

items.example: The meeting took place shortly after midday.
items.note: An event takes place; past tense took place.

items.example: Witnesses could not identify the attacker.
items.note: Person who attacks another person or place; related to attack.

items.example: Everyone escaped from the damaged building.
items.note: Can be a verb or noun; escape from a place is common.

items.example: The thieves got away before the police arrived.
items.note: Informal alternative to escape in this context; past got away.

items.example: The frightened children hid behind a wall.
items.note: Past tense hid and past participle hidden; hide from someone.

items.example: The dog was hiding under the table.
items.note: Present participle of hide, also in be hiding.

items.example: The officer did not shoot because people were nearby.
items.note: The past tense and past participle of shoot are shot.

items.pt: atingido por disparo; baleado; passado de shoot
items.example: The injured bird had been shot.
items.note: Past tense or past participle of shoot; also a noun meaning a gunshot or attempt.

items.example: The old dog died peacefully last year.
items.note: Intransitive verb: a person dies, but something kills a person.

items.example: Doctors confirmed that the animal was dead.
items.note: Adjective, not a past tense verb: is dead or was dead.

items.example: The news reported the death of a local resident.
items.note: Noun related to die and dead; plural deaths.

items.example: The authorities reported no deaths after the accident.
items.note: Plural of death; used for a count of people who died.

items.example: One hiker is still missing after the storm.
items.note: Missing means the person's whereabouts are not known; not simply lost.

items.pt: estar desaparecido; estar em local desconhecido
items.example: A passenger was reported to be missing.
items.note: A common reporting construction for people whose location is unknown.

items.example: Two officers were on patrol when they received the call.
items.note: Being out to check or protect an area.

items.example: A brief gun battle was reported on the outskirts.
items.note: A period of fighting in which guns are used.

items.pt: ter previsão de aumento; esperar-se que aumente
items.example: Prices are expected to rise again next month.
items.note: The passive reporting pattern be expected to + infinitive expresses a prediction.

items.example: The number of visitors may rise in summer.
items.note: Intransitive change: rise, rose, risen; not raise something.

sectionsChecked: A: The job of the army; labelled soldiers, guns, defence, war and battle, and violence/violent language help
B: Reporting in war; news-panel vocabulary, numbered definitions and verb/noun language help
Exercises 59.1–59.5 and answer key; word class, contrasting meanings, past forms and protect/protection, destroy/destruction, explode/explosion, defend/defence families

units.title: Unit 60 — Time
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 126–127 (PDF pages 127–128).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish in time and on time, and use common phrases for available time and occasions.
Choose by, until, for, since, during and in with appropriate deadlines, durations and time points.
Use approximate past, present and future expressions such as for ages, the other day and for the time being.
Name time units from seconds to centuries, including the British term fortnight.
Distinguish how long an activity takes from how long an event lasts.

items.pt: a tempo; antes de ser tarde
items.example: We got to the airport in time for our flight.
items.note: Early enough for something to happen; not necessarily exactly at the scheduled time.

items.example: The meeting started on time despite the rain.
items.note: At the arranged or scheduled time, neither early nor late.

items.example: It's time to go, or we'll miss the bus.
items.note: Pattern: it's time to + infinitive; for a named person, it's time for someone to do something.

items.example: Do you have time to look at this document?
items.note: Have enough available time; can be followed by to + infinitive.

items.example: We have time for a quick coffee before the train.
items.note: Pattern have time for + noun; a related pattern is have time to + verb.

items.example: The next time you visit, we can have lunch together.
items.note: Refers to the next occasion on which something happens.

items.pt: da última vez; na última ocasião
items.example: The last time I saw her, she was working in London.
items.note: Refers to the most recent previous occasion.

items.example: Both trains arrived at the same time.
items.note: Two events occur together or at the same clock time.

items.example: We chose the same day for our appointments.
items.note: Usually used with the: the same time, the same day.

items.pt: até; até o momento em que
items.example: The library stays open until six o'clock.
items.note: An action or state continues up to a time; not the same as a deadline with by.

items.example: Please send the report by Friday.
items.note: Expresses a deadline: no later than that time; does not mean continued duration.

items.pt: até segunda-feira; no máximo na segunda-feira
items.example: The documents need to be ready by Monday.
items.note: A concrete deadline phrase illustrating by + a point in time.

items.example: She worked at the museum for six months.
items.note: Follow for with a duration, such as six months or two years.

items.example: I've lived here since 2021.
items.note: Use since with a starting point or clause in the past, not a duration.

items.example: We met several local people during our holiday.
items.note: Follow during with an event or named period; use for to say how long something lasted.

items.pt: por seis meses; há seis meses (conforme o tempo verbal)
items.example: They have lived in the city for six months.
items.note: Duration with for; contrasts with since + starting point.

items.example: I've known my neighbour since May.
items.note: Point-of-time phrase; not for May when giving a starting point.

items.example: They worked on a farm during the summer.
items.note: Answers when the activity happened; not how many weeks it lasted.

items.example: I'll be back in ten days' time.
items.note: Means ten days from now; not after ten days' time.

items.example: Our new office will open in three months' time.
items.note: Another example of in + duration + time for a future point.

items.example: The shop closed for a short period of time.
items.note: A duration rather than a single point on the calendar.

items.example: The date marks a specific point in time.
items.note: The type of reference used after since, unlike a duration after for.

items.pt: há muito tempo; por muito tempo
items.example: I haven't seen my old friends for ages.
items.note: Informal phrase for a very long period, especially with perfect tenses.

items.example: She recently started a new job.
items.note: At a time not long before now; usable with different verb tenses.

items.example: Have you spoken to your sister lately?
items.note: Often used with the present perfect for a recent period up to now.

items.pt: há muito tempo; faz muito tempo
items.example: They moved abroad a long time ago.
items.note: A point well in the past; normally used with a past tense.

items.pt: há muito tempo; há uma eternidade (informal)
items.example: I read that novel ages ago.
items.note: Informal equivalent to a long time ago; refers to a past event.

items.example: I met our old teacher the other day.
items.note: An unspecified day in the recent past.

items.example: These days, I prefer travelling by train.
items.note: The general present period, often contrasting with the past.

items.example: Nowadays, many people work from home.
items.note: General present time; similar to these days.

items.example: For the time being, we'll use the smaller meeting room.
items.note: A temporary arrangement that may change later.

items.pt: algum dia; um dia no futuro
items.example: One day, I hope to visit Japan.
items.note: An indefinite future point; context can also make one day refer to the past.

items.pt: não faz muito tempo; há pouco tempo
items.example: I spoke to the manager not long ago.
items.note: An approximate time shortly before now; offered in the source's explanation of recently.

items.example: I'm busy at the moment, but I can call later.
items.note: Expresses the current point or current period; useful contrast to nowadays.

items.example: Wait a second while I check the answer.
items.note: Unit of time; sixty seconds make one minute.

items.example: The video lasts just one minute.
items.note: A minute contains sixty seconds.

items.example: The journey took about an hour.
items.note: An hour contains sixty minutes; h is silent.

items.example: The course takes place one day a week.
items.note: A standard day has twenty-four hours.

items.example: We have an English lesson every week.
items.note: A week has seven days.

items.example: We're going on holiday for a fortnight.
items.note: British English for a period of two weeks, or fourteen days.

items.example: The project took about a month to complete.
items.note: A calendar period of roughly four weeks; the number of days varies.

items.example: She has studied English for a year.
items.note: A calendar year normally has twelve months.

items.example: The town changed a lot over the last decade.
items.note: A period of ten years.

items.example: That bridge was built in the nineteenth century.
items.note: A period of one hundred years; use ordinal numbers for named centuries.

items.example: Several important developments occurred in the 1960s.
items.note: Refers to a calendar decade; pronunciation uses the plural sixties.

items.example: It can take several hours to repair the machine.
items.note: For duration needed to do something, use it takes + someone + time + to + verb.

items.pt: leva meia hora; demora trinta minutos
items.example: It takes half an hour to walk to the station.
items.note: Pattern used to say how much time is needed to complete an activity.

items.pt: quanto tempo leva?; quanto tempo demora?
items.example: How long does it take to reach the airport?
items.note: Ask about time needed to do or complete something.

items.example: The concert lasted nearly two hours.
items.note: For the duration of an event, not the time someone needs to do a task.

items.example: The training course will last for ten weeks.
items.note: Last for + duration; for is often optional after last.

items.example: How long does the performance last?
items.note: Asks about how long an event continues, not the time needed to finish a task.

items.example: The batteries didn't last long in the cold.
items.note: A natural expression for continuing or remaining useful over time.

sectionsChecked: A: Phrases with time; on time, in time, enough time, next/last time and same time
B: Preposition contrasts; until/by, for/since, during/for, in ... time and related common mistakes
C: Approximate periods of time; past, present and future expressions
D: Counting time; seconds, minutes, days, weeks, fortnight, year, decade and century
E: Take and last; contrasting duration constructions
Exercises 60.1–60.5 and Unit 60 answer key; fixed phrases, prepositions, approximate time and number terminology
